item.title: The Daily Star – The forgotten story of how Ekushey inspired language activism in West Pakistan
item.description:
The Bengali Language Movement of 1952 was not the only challenge to Pakistan's Urdu-centric language policy. Across West Pakistan, writers, intellectuals and political activists also resisted linguistic centralisation, demanding recognition for Punjabi, Sindhi and Pashto. Yet these movements differed in their political ambitions, strategies and relationships with the Pakistani state. In an interview with The Daily Star, French historian and writer Julien Columeau, author of Linguistic Resistance in Pakistan: Punjabi Language Movements After Independence (Columbia University Press, 2026), discusses this overlooked history, the influence of Ekushey February on Punjabi activists and the wider struggle for linguistic rights in Pakistan.

The Daily Star (TDS): What first drew you to the study of language movements and linguistic resistance in post-1947 Pakistan, particularly the Punjabi language movement?

Julien Columeau (JC): I have always been interested in language policy issues, especially the dichotomy between vernacular and national languages, undoubtedly because the region of France I come from predominantly spoke a vernacular language (Occitan), which was gradually replaced by French, both through the will of the state and due to people's negative attitudes towards their language, which they had been led to consider backward. A movement was launched to protect Occitan, but it did not achieve the desired results. After I moved to Pakistan, I found in Punjab an interesting situation, which reminded me to some extent of my own region. 

Without necessarily thinking, like Dr Olga Khokhlova, that Punjabi will die and be replaced by Urdu, one cannot deny that millions of Punjabi speakers are gradually switching to Urdu, and the gains obtained by activists remain symbolic, generating a paradoxical situation: Punjabi is not used as a medium of instruction in the province's schools, but one can do a PhD in Punjabi at university.

TDS: At the time of Partition in 1947, Urdu was the mother tongue of only about 3 per cent of Pakistan's population, while Bengali was spoken by more than 55 per cent. Why was Pakistan's ruling elite determined to establish Urdu as the sole national language?

JC: There are several factors, which I discuss in detail in my book, including the desire to merge linguistic and religious identity, and the fact that vernacular languages did not seem 'Islamic' enough in the eyes of activists like Baba-e-Urdu Maulvi Abdul Haq, who influenced the country's language policy: Bengali, with its vocabulary largely derived from Sanskrit and its script derived from Brahmi, did not appear Islamic enough to them, nor did Punjabi, which was labelled the 'language of the Sikhs'. 
Maulvi Abdul Haq (second from left), a prominent advocate of Urdu as Pakistan's national language. Following the Bengali Language Movement of 1952, he moderated his earlier position, acknowledging that the development of Urdu should not come at the expense of regional languages.

There was also a conviction among some activists that Urdu, even though it was the language of only 3% of Pakistanis, would become, within a few generations, the language of the majority, who would abandon their vernaculars in favour of Urdu, in the same way that the populations of North Africa, after being Islamised, had abandoned their vernaculars in favour of Arabic. Punjab, because of its elites' sympathy for Urdu and its pro-Urdu policies, seemed to these activists to be the province where this ‘great replacement’ of the vernacular language by the national language would have the best chance of taking place.

TDS: How did the government and the public in West Pakistan, particularly Punjab, react to the killing of students during the Bengali Language Movement on 21 February 1952?

JC: While the government's reaction was unanimously hostile, the public, at least in Punjab province, which is my subject of study, was divided. 

Left-wing circles were certainly shocked and outraged, and Ekushey rallied their solidarity with the Bengalis and their cause. Conservative circles had to acknowledge the Bengalis' determination to die for their language and that the inclusion of Bengali in the constitution was inevitable. 

Confronted with such determination, even a staunch activist like Maulvi Abdul Haq had to change his position regarding the unconditional imposition of Urdu: during the second Urdu conference held in Karachi only two months after Ekushey, he stated that the development of Urdu should not come at the expense of vernacular languages (whereas during the first conference in 1948, he had declared that none were worth developing).
Students prepare to defy Section 144 at Dhaka University's Old Arts Building on 21 February 1952. The Bengali Language Movement subsequently inspired Punjabi activists in West Pakistan, who began observing the anniversary in Lahore to press for recognition of their own mother tongue. Photo: Rafiqul Islam

TDS: Punjabi language activists later began observing 21 February in Lahore. How did the Bengali Language Movement influence their demands, strategies and understanding of linguistic rights?

JC: The Bengali movement inspired Punjabi activists by demonstrating that linguistic demands could mobilise public opinion and challenge the state's national ideology. It also showed that defending a vernacular language could be compatible with loyalty to Pakistan. However, Punjabi activists generally adopted more cautious demands. The position of Punjab's elites and the strong association between Urdu and Pakistani national identity constrained their ambitions. They sought greater recognition for Punjabi while avoiding accusations of undermining national unity, particularly through demands for constitutional recognition or an administrative role. The Punjabi activists adapted the Bengali example to their own political and ideological environment.
The cover of Linguistic Resistance in Pakistan: Punjabi Language Movements After Independence by historian Julien Columeau (Columbia University Press, 2026). The book explores the struggle for recognition of Punjabi and its connections with the Bengali Language Movement and wider linguistic resistance in Pakistan.

TDS: Punjabi activists were frequently accused of being anti-Pakistan or sympathetic to India and the Sikhs. How did they respond to these accusations while advocating recognition for their mother tongue?

JC: This accusation of being anti-national or anti-Pakistan weighed heavily on all Punjabi activists, regardless of their political affiliation. They were accused of being complicit with the Sikhs, who had been the main champions of Punjabi, and of wanting to diminish the role of Urdu. They therefore resorted to various strategies: to show that there was no antagonism between Urdu and Punjabi, they declared that Urdu descended from Punjabi (and, thus, serving the Punjabi cause was tantamount to serving the Urdu cause), or they proposed to Pakistanise Punjabi, purging it of lexical and cultural elements that could be identified as being linked to Sikhs, thereby promoting an Urduised version called Pak Punjabi. 

Others, finally, offered assurances that their movement would not go the Bengali way and that they were demanding neither that Punjabi be enshrined in the constitution nor that it be given the administrative role that belonged to Urdu.

TDS: Beyond East Bengal and Punjab, how did linguistic movements in Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province challenge Urdu's dominance? To what extent did these movements cooperate with Bengali activists?

JC: Punjabi activism formed part of a broader landscape of linguistic resistance. Strong movements also emerged in Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province, now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, associated with figures such as G. M. Syed and Bacha Khan. Their demands could be more radical than those of Punjabi activists, reflecting different regional histories and aspirations for cultural autonomy. Despite their strength, these movements achieved limited results in the early post-partition period. Symbolic recognition did not necessarily challenge Urdu's dominance in public institutions. Nor did regional movements consistently coordinate their efforts with the Bengali movement during the first years after independence. 

The creation of the National Awami Party (NAP) subsequently brought together political forces advocating regional rights and opposing centralisation, creating new possibilities for cooperation. These experiences demonstrate that shared linguistic grievances do not automatically produce solidarity; political alliances require organisation and the negotiation of different regional priorities.
Saadat Hasan Manto, the celebrated Urdu writer who reportedly considered writing in Punjabi. According to Julien Columeau, Manto even wrote a long story in Punjabi, but the manuscript was lost following his untimely death.

TDS: Despite their progressive political outlook, prominent Lahore-based writers such as Faiz Ahmad Faiz and Saadat Hasan Manto primarily wrote in Urdu. What explains their different attitudes towards writing in Punjabi?

JC: Faiz and Manto had very different temperaments, and their attitudes towards Punjabi were therefore different. Faiz was tempted in the early 1950s to write in Punjabi (he mentions this in a letter from prison to his wife) in order to communicate with the masses, but he gave up on the idea. It wasn't until the 1970s that he wrote a few poems in Punjabi. Safdar Mir and Ashfaq Tanwir Mirza attribute this renunciation of writing in Punjabi to a fear of social demotion, as writing in Urdu was a means of social and cultural advancement. 

Manto, on the other hand, even though he was an author who had made a name for himself writing in Urdu, did not seem to fear social demotion and reportedly considered embarking on a career as a Punjabi writer, even writing a long story in Punjabi. Unfortunately, his untimely death prevented him from realising this project, and his story has been lost.

TDS: How does examining the language movements of West Pakistan alongside the Bengali Language Movement help us better understand Pakistan's early history, particularly the relationship between language, national identity and political power?

JC: Studying Punjabi activism allows us to reconsider Pakistan's history beyond the dichotomy of an oppressive West Pakistan and an oppressed East Pakistan. Many intellectuals, writers and politicians in West Pakistan challenged their government's language policies and defended regional linguistic identities. Punjabi, Sindhi and Pashtun movements opposed aspects of linguistic centralisation, even if their demands and methods differed from those of Bengali activists. 
Pak Tea House in Lahore, a historic gathering place for writers, poets and intellectuals. The city's literary circles played an important role in debates over language, cultural identity and the dominance of Urdu in post-Partition Pakistan.

Pakistan's language politics should therefore be understood not simply as a confrontation between West and East Pakistan, but as a history of resistance within both regions. Ultimately, I believe the significance of West Pakistan's movements lies not only in their immediate achievements but also in the fact that they continued to challenge the government's assumption that national unity requires linguistic uniformity. Punjabi activism, despite its limitations, reveals how citizens and intellectuals contested linguistic hierarchies and imagined alternative relationships between language, identity and political community.

The interview was taken by Adrin Sarwar.

item.title: The Daily Star – Robert Pattinson's James Bond and the masculinity of a new era
item.description:
James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era.

Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s.

In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged.

Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma.

Pattinson’s career

Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles.

From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective.

There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig.

Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024.
 
Sean Connery and Pierce Brosnan played Bonds that reflected their times, so what will Robert Pattinson’s look like? 007/Alamy/Collection Christophel/Everett Collection Inc

Pattinson’s Bond 

As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity.

In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity.

I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond.

Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity.

Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability.

Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture.

In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced.

I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim.

This article was first published under the title “Bond has always reflected the masculinity of his time – Robert Pattinson’s 007 will need to embody a new era.” in The Conversation, on November 17, 2026.

Monica Germanà is Reader in Gothic and Contemporary Studies, University of Westminster.

item.title: The Daily Star – ICJ verdict against Myanmar: What next for the Rohingya and Bangladesh?
item.description:
In a historic judgment delivered on November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found Myanmar responsible for genocide against its Rohingya population during the military's brutal 2016–2017 operations in Rakhine State. After years of legal proceedings and nearly a decade of international inaction, the verdict has brought renewed attention to a humanitarian catastrophe that was gradually slipping from the world's consciousness. The judgment marks a watershed moment in the pursuit of accountability for the atrocities committed against the Rohingya, following a seven-year legal battle initiated by the Gambia in 2019.

The significance of this ruling extends well beyond its immediate legal implications. For the first time, the ICJ has found a state responsible for committing genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention. The case is also remarkable because it was brought by the Gambia, a small West African country with no direct geographical or political stake in the Rohingya crisis, demonstrating how states can invoke international law to uphold collective obligations against genocide. The judgment further acknowledges the scale and systematic nature of the violence, including the killing of thousands of Rohingya civilians, widespread sexual violence and attacks on children, and the “intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population” through acts of ethnic cleansing.

For Bangladesh, which opened its borders to hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fleeing military persecution in 2017, the ruling carries particular significance. It reinforces the international legitimacy of Bangladesh's humanitarian response and strengthens its diplomatic position in advocating for a durable solution. But what does this judgment mean for the more than one million Rohingya refugees who remain stranded in Bangladesh? More importantly, how can the Rohingya community, the Bangladesh government and the international community translate this legal victory into meaningful political and practical outcomes?

From legal recognition to accountability

The ICJ judgment is legally binding on Myanmar under Article 59 of the Court's Statute and Article 94(1) of the UN Charter. Myanmar is obliged to comply with the Court's decision. Under Article 94(2), the Gambia, as the applicant state, can bring alleged non-compliance before the UN Security Council, which may recommend or decide on measures to give effect to the judgment. However, the Court has no independent enforcement mechanism, and the political dynamics of the Security Council, particularly the possibility of a veto, remain significant obstacles.
Judge Yuji Iwasawa, president of the International Court of Justice (ICJ), presides over the delivery of the Court's landmark judgment in the Rohingya genocide case brought against Myanmar by the Gambia in The Hague, Netherlands, on 19 November 2026. The ruling marks a significant step towards international accountability for atrocities committed against the Rohingya. Photo: Reuters

The judgment also unfolds against an increasingly complicated political landscape in Myanmar. The military government at the centre, the Arakan Army, which now exercises de facto control over substantial parts of Rakhine State, the epicentre of the Rohingya genocide, and the exiled National Unity Government (NUG), largely led by exiled politicians from Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy (NLD), represent different centres of political and military power. Their positions and responses to the judgment will have important implications for the Rohingya's future. The Arakan Army, in particular, cannot be excluded from any discussion of protection, rights and eventual repatriation, given its growing territorial influence and reported abuses against Rohingya communities.

It is too early to predict how these actors will respond. item.title: The Daily Star – Bengal, India, and parasitic imperialism: How America helped sustain the British Raj
item.description:
In an issue of the Vancouver-based newspaper The Province from 18 October 1907, one can find a four-tiered headline that reads as follows: “India Generally Free From Political Unrest. Some Disappointed Agitators Are Trying to Make Trouble in Bengal. England’s Rule Praised. American Missionary Says Situation Has Been Misrepresented.”

The American missionary in question was a certain Rev. William Moyser, who had stopped in Vancouver on his way back to his hometown of Portland, Oregon, after working in India for thirteen years. The journalist had asked Moyser for his opinion on the anti-Asian riots that had engulfed the West Coast of North America that year, as well as on rumours about anti-British agitation in India. Moyser responds that he was not as familiar with the West Coast context but could speak to the Indian one, of which he says that—contrary to the many misrepresentations—there is no general unrest in the country, except perhaps in Bengal, where the agitators are merely “disgruntled over the fact that they have not been able to obtain every lucrative office they may have desired.” Moyser conveniently glosses over the infamous Partition of Bengal just two years earlier—more on that in due course—and its role in the agitation. He goes on to dispel any fears that there is a mass exodus of Indians from the subcontinent to North America, or that the British are levying exorbitant taxes on the people. 

He ends with the following admission: “Now, I am an American citizen, and not a subject of Great Britain, so I cannot be accused of saying these things to shield a Government of which some one might hastily conclude me to be a citizen, but I cannot keep still when I hear the untrue and unjust things that have been said about the country in which I am so vitally interested.”

What are we to make of this American missionary defending the British imperial project in India, a project in which he is so “vitally interested”? And what do we make of the fact that Moyser is so hyper-aware of his being misconstrued as a British citizen by virtue of his race and language?
 
An article in the Vancouver-based newspaper The Province, published on 18 October 1907, features an American missionary defending British rule in India and dismissing political unrest in Bengal. Beside it, an illustration of American heiress Gladys Vanderbilt highlights the transatlantic elite connections that also shaped British imperialism. Image: The Province

To a seasoned historian of transatlantic relations, Moyser’s statement would be unsurprising. This is because, in the late nineteenth century, there had transpired what we have come to know as the “Great Rapprochement”, a geopolitical event wherein Britain and the United States came to increasingly recognise each other as two branches of the same ancestral tree, united by a shared Anglo-Saxon race, common law, language, and customs. However, in many accounts of this “great white reunion”, what falls out of view is another shared burden, a burden that Kipling identified as possibly the greatest for the white man: empire. More specifically, histories of the Rapprochement and of imperialism do not adequately illustrate the extent to which American state and non-state actors—such as missionaries like Moyser—were integral to the fabric of British imperialism. This has been a question that has plagued me since my own upbringing and education in Pakistan, where—as I imagine it is in Bangladesh as well—the history of British colonialism in the subcontinent is taught in an insular fashion. In such historiography, the Pax Americana suddenly cycles past the Pax Britannica in the mid-century, as if the former did not practise with its training wheels in the playgrounds of the latter. Newer histories, such as those by Seema Sohi and Stephen Tuffnell, seek to disrupt this very insularity and give more global accounts of inter-imperial collaboration, and my own seeks to build on those. In fact, Sohi’s book—on the Ghadar Party’s resistance against Britain from the West Coast of North America—would powerfully contextualise the above newspaper article.

Just adjacent to that article is an illustration of Gladys Vanderbilt and her fiancé, the Hungarian Count Szechenyi, riding in a carriage in Newport, Rhode Island. “Vanderbilt Wedding Will Be Very Gay Society Event,” it says above the illustration, accompanied by a short caption that tells us that Gladys is heir to $15,000,000.

The illustration caught my eye not just because of how HBO’s The Gilded Age (now in its fourth season, released just at the beginning of this month) has fictionalised the life of Gladys and the Vanderbilts, but also because British India was home to its own “dollar princess” at the time: Mary Leiter Curzon, wife of Viceroy Curzon, the very same man who partitioned Bengal in 1905. 

“Dollar princesses” were American heiresses who married into European—especially British—nobility, the immense wealth they brought helping to keep their new husbands’ estates running. Mary Leiter was one of these so-called princesses, except she came to the rescue of not just Curzon’s marquessate of Kedleston but India itself, using her influence in Chicago’s elite circles to fundraise for famine and plague relief in India.
 
Lord and Lady Curzon during their tour of Oman, Kuwait and other Persian Gulf ports in November and December 1903. As Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon sought to expand British imperial influence in the region, while his American-born wife, Mary Curzon, exemplified the transatlantic connections that helped sustain the British Raj. Photo: Unknown photographer

Missionaries like Moyser and dollar princesses like Mary Curzon were therefore two examples of non-state American figures woven inextricably into the Raj’s imperial tapestry. What interested me in the writing of Parasitic Empires, however, was the involvement of such figures more specifically in a medicalised and public health-related imperial collaboration, which I call “parasitic imperialism”. I define this as the ways in which “white English-speaking or Anglo-Saxon empires in the long twentieth century collaborated and competed with one another through racially inflected discourses of hygiene and infectious disease management, thereby reconfiguring Anglophone whiteness itself.” To be sure, both the American vicereine and American medical missionaries were heavily invested in such health-related discourses of the liberal civilising mission. Mary Curzon, apart from her fundraising activities, was closely associated with the Dufferin Fund for native Indian women’s health, and missionaries like William Wanless, associated with the Presbyterian Church of Philadelphia, established missionary medical schools, leprosaria, and tuberculosis sanatoriums in Western India.

Anglophone parasitic imperialism became especially conspicuous through the work of missionaries and social hygiene activists who sought to curb prostitution and venereal disease. For instance, American missionary and doctor Katherine Bushnell and her colleague Elizabeth Andrew collaborated with the British reformer Josephine Butler to conduct research on the Contagious Diseases Acts in India; these Acts codified the regulation of sex work in India and the incarceration of prostitutes in “lock hospitals” if they were found to be infected with venereal disease. Their exposé was published as The Queen’s Daughters in India in 1898, the very year the United States acquired its own maritime empire in the Caribbean and the Pacific in the wake of the Spanish-American War. Fast forward to the 1920s, and another, more infamous American woman—Katherine Mayo—published Mother India (1926), an even more controversial book that condemned and sensationalised the Hindus’ so-called depraved sexual practices and defended the British imperial presence in India. In fact, the book opens with a lurid description of the worship of Kali at a Calcutta temple.
 
Cover of Bassam Sidiki’s Parasitic Empires: Infection, Insularity, Inter-Imperiality, 1880–2022 (University of North Carolina Press, 2026), which examines how medicine, infectious disease and racial politics shaped collaboration and competition between British and American empires.

Interestingly, Bushnell’s and Mayo’s accounts are haunted by the spectre of the “white slave trade”, which was the trafficking of European women for prostitution. This was an especially huge problem in the colonies because the presence of European sex workers—and the possibility of sexual congress with non-white men—would be incredibly damaging to white prestige. America and Britain collaborated very closely through social hygiene associations to halt the white slave trade. Bombay and Calcutta were known to have a small number of European prostitutes. However, no mention is made of them in Bushnell’s and Mayo’s writings. For instance, in 1901, Sir John Woodburn, the Lieutenant Governor of Bengal, passed an order forbidding the employment of European barmaids in Calcutta. This was the first in a long line of legal actions that led to the passage of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic Act (SITA) in Calcutta in 1923.

In Parasitic Empires, I argue that one can read E. M. Forster’s famous novel A Passage to India (1924) by contextualising it within this inter-imperial history of legislation against the white slave trade. Those familiar with the novel will remember that after the Muslim physician Dr Aziz is accused of sexually assaulting the British woman Adela Quested in the Marabar Caves, the prosecution produces evidence of Aziz wanting to visit brothels in Calcutta to prove his immoral character. Against the backdrop of possible white prostitutes in Calcutta, Dr Aziz’s intentions become even more questionable, with the result that Adela Quested becomes not a chaste English girl but a fallen colonial woman.
 
First edition cover of E. M. Forster’s A Passage to India (1924), a novel that explores racial tensions and colonial power in British India, including anxieties surrounding sexuality and the perceived threat to white prestige.

A Passage to India was published a year before American novelist Sinclair Lewis’s Arrowsmith (1925), which I also read as another node in what I call an “inter-imperial social hygiene network”, given that the latter text, like Forster’s, includes references to social vice, venereal disease, and white women in the colonies. The colony in question here is not India but a fictional Caribbean island under British control named St Hubert, where the protagonist Martin Arrowsmith, an American bacteriologist, is sent by the McGurk Institute to fight bubonic plague. The McGurk Institute is Lewis’s fictionalised version of the Rockefeller Foundation’s International Health Board (IHB). The IHB, I argue, was the last but perhaps the most important instantiation of parasitic imperialism. As historian Steven Palmer suggests, the IHB was like a “parasite”, using British colonial possessions in the Caribbean to conduct its research on tropical diseases like hookworm. Bengal and India writ large also played host to the IHB’s parasitological activities, a major representative of which was the physician John B. Grant.

Grant was born to Canadian missionaries in China in 1890 and, after being educated at the University of Michigan and Johns Hopkins, went on to have an illustrious career in public and global health. As part of the Rockefeller Foundation’s IHB, he conducted hookworm surveys in China and, in 1921, became an associate professor of public health at Peking Union Medical College, a medical school that the Rockefeller Foundation itself helped establish in 1917. After his time in China concluded in 1939, Grant was appointed director of the All-India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health in Calcutta, a role in which he served until 1945. He was also associated with the famous Bhore Committee of 1944, which laid the foundation for medical care and public health in independent India.
 
Cover of The Queen’s Daughters in India by Elizabeth W. Andrew and Katherine C. Bushnell (1898), an exposé of prostitution and the regulation of sex work under British colonial rule, highlighting the role of American reformers in imperial debates over public health and morality.

John Grant’s work in India shows, however, that Anglophone parasitic imperialism was not just about collaboration but also about rivalry and competition. Like many of his fellow Rockefeller associates stationed in British territories, Grant regularly critiqued the British colonial status quo and bemoaned the conservatism, inefficiency, and backwardness of the Indian Medical Service. It is notable that after Grant retired from the Rockefeller Foundation, he settled in San Juan, Puerto Rico—an American, not British, colonial acquisition—where he advised the government on the coordination of its medical services. Grant’s work in Puerto Rico would have been contemporaneous with the horrific, unfettered sterilisation of Puerto Rican women that the US government had been conducting for decades. 

As far as we know, Grant was not in any way affiliated with these practices, but his inter-imperial medical itinerary—from China to India to Puerto Rico, born to Canadians and becoming a naturalised American—testifies to how knowledge of health and disease moved across multiple imperial spheres of influence and was transformed in the process, even as it engendered simultaneous collaboration and competition between the imperial actors in question. Rockefeller Foundation doctors—like missionaries, dollar princesses, and social hygiene activists—were, therefore, yet another group of agents of parasitic imperialism in the long twentieth century.

Bassam Sidiki is an assistant professor of English at the University of Texas at Austin. He is the author of Parasitic Empires: Infection, Insularity, Inter-Imperiality, 1880–2022 (UNC Press, 2026) and Literature and War Medicine (Cambridge Elements in Health Humanities, 2026).

A Passage to India was published a year before American novelist Sinclair Lewis’s Arrowsmith (1925), which I also read as another node in what I call an “inter-imperial social hygiene network”, given that the latter text, like Forster’s, includes references to social vice, venereal disease, and white women in the colonies. The colony in question here is not India but a fictional Caribbean island under British control named St Hubert, where the protagonist Martin Arrowsmith, an American bacteriologist, is sent by the McGurk Institute to fight bubonic plague. The McGurk Institute is Lewis’s fictionalised version of the Rockefeller Foundation’s International Health Board (IHB). The IHB, I argue, was the last but perhaps the most important instantiation of parasitic imperialism. As historian Steven Palmer suggests, the IHB was like a “parasite”, using British colonial possessions in the Caribbean to conduct its research on tropical diseases like hookworm. Bengal and India writ large also played host to the IHB’s parasitological activities, a major representative of which was the physician John B. Grant.

Grant was born to Canadian missionaries in China in 1890 and, after being educated at the University of Michigan and Johns Hopkins, went on to have an illustrious career in public and global health. As part of the Rockefeller Foundation’s IHB, he conducted hookworm surveys in China and, in 1921, became an associate professor of public health at Peking Union Medical College, a medical school that the Rockefeller Foundation itself helped establish in 1917. After his time in China concluded in 1939, Grant was appointed director of the All-India Institute of Hygiene and Public Health in Calcutta, a role in which he served until 1945. He was also associated with the famous Bhore Committee of 1944, which laid the foundation for medical care and public health in independent India.
 
Cover of The Queen’s Daughters in India by Elizabeth W. Andrew and Katherine C. Bushnell (1898), an exposé of prostitution and the regulation of sex work under British colonial rule, highlighting the role of American reformers in imperial debates over public health and morality.

John Grant’s work in India shows, however, that Anglophone parasitic imperialism was not just about collaboration but also about rivalry and competition. Like many of his fellow Rockefeller associates stationed in British territories, Grant regularly critiqued the British colonial status quo and bemoaned the conservatism, inefficiency, and backwardness of the Indian Medical Service. It is notable that after Grant retired from the Rockefeller Foundation, he settled in San Juan, Puerto Rico—an American, not British, colonial acquisition—where he advised the government on the coordination of its medical services. Grant’s work in Puerto Rico would have been contemporaneous with the horrific, unfettered sterilisation of Puerto Rican women that the US government had been conducting for decades. 

As far as we know, Grant was not in any way affiliated with these practices, but his inter-imperial medical itinerary—from China to India to Puerto Rico, born to Canadians and becoming a naturalised American—testifies to how knowledge of health and disease moved across multiple imperial spheres of influence and was transformed in the process, even as it engendered simultaneous collaboration and competition between the imperial actors in question. Rockefeller Foundation doctors—like missionaries, dollar princesses, and social hygiene activists—were, therefore, yet another group of agents of parasitic imperialism in the long twentieth century.

item.title: The Daily Star – Preventing a lost generation: Preparing Rohingya youth for return and reconstruction
item.description:
As the Rohingya crisis approaches its tenth year, Bangladesh continues to shoulder one of the world's largest and most complex humanitarian responsibilities by hosting more than one million Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals (FDMNs), despite its own demographic, environmental and economic constraints. The Government of Bangladesh has consistently reaffirmed that voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable repatriation to Myanmar remains the only durable solution. However, prolonged displacement has transformed what was initially an emergency into a protracted crisis with profound humanitarian, developmental, educational and security implications.

The judgment of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Gambia v. Myanmar represents a significant development in the international pursuit of justice and accountability for the Rohingya. The case, initiated in November 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, concerns allegations that Myanmar violated its international obligations in relation to the Rohingya. While the judgment will not, in itself, resolve the political and practical challenges of repatriation, it may carry important implications for international accountability, the recognition of Rohingya rights and the broader conditions necessary for a sustainable return. It also reinforces the importance of preparing the Rohingya community for a future in which justice, security and meaningful participation must accompany repatriation.

Within this context, education has emerged as one of the most critical pillars of the response. Beyond fulfilling a fundamental human right, quality education serves as a strategic instrument for preserving identity, protecting children from exploitation, strengthening social cohesion, developing future leadership and preparing refugees for meaningful participation in the reconstruction of Myanmar. Ensuring educational continuity, therefore, requires more than expanding access to learning centres. It demands an integrated approach encompassing quality education, cultural preservation, language proficiency, digital competencies, higher education and community ownership, while remaining consistent with Bangladesh's repatriation-centred policy.

Against this backdrop, the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC), representing the Government of Bangladesh in coordinating the refugee response, has increasingly facilitated initiatives extending beyond conventional humanitarian education. Through institutional coordination, policy facilitation and partnerships with UN agencies, academic institutions, NGOs and Rohingya community-led educational organisations, the RRRC has contributed to developing a diversified educational ecosystem. This paper examines the existing educational landscape, identifies emerging challenges, highlights the RRRC's strategic initiatives and proposes policy recommendations for strengthening education as an instrument of sustainable repatriation and long-term regional stability.

Overview of educational activities and emerging gaps

The Education Sector in the Rohingya response in Cox's Bazar is one of the world's largest humanitarian education initiatives, jointly coordinated by UNICEF and Save the Children International in collaboration with 42 implementing partners. According to the 2026 Joint Response Plan (JRP), approximately 769,799 Rohingya and host-community children and adolescents require educational assistance, while 488,344 learners are targeted for educational services. The sector operates through 6,252 educational facilities, including 3,726 learning centres, supported by approximately 8,136 volunteer teachers.

The learning centres follow the Myanmar Curriculum Framework, providing an important foundation for future educational continuity and reintegration into Myanmar. Nevertheless, several curricular and institutional limitations undermine the inclusiveness and long-term relevance of the current arrangements.

First, the curriculum does not adequately accommodate Rohingya history, identity and the historical significance of Arakan. The absence of systematic opportunities to learn about their own heritage may weaken younger generations' connection with their historical roots. Similarly, the limited inclusion of Islamic Studies and the Rohingya language constrains the preservation of religious, linguistic and cultural identity. Science education also remains largely theoretical because of inadequate laboratory facilities and practical experimentation, while limited access to computers and digital technologies restricts the acquisition of essential twenty-first-century competencies.

A particularly significant gap is the absence of a comprehensive and recognised assessment and certification system across the learning-centre network. Although students participate in structured educational activities, their learning outcomes are not consistently assessed through standardised mechanisms, nor do they routinely receive formally recognised certificates upon completing different educational levels. Consequently, years of learning may not translate into demonstrable qualifications, potentially undermining further educational progression, skills development and future reintegration. This uncertainty may also contribute to declining learner motivation and increased dropout rates.
Shah Alam, 22, who fled Myanmar before completing high school, teaches Rohingya children at Kutupalong camp after receiving training as a volunteer educator. His journey highlights the importance of teacher development and educational continuity in preparing displaced Rohingya youth for the future. Photo: UNHCR/Amos Halder

To address these gaps, learning centres should continue implementing the Myanmar Curriculum while incorporating supplementary content on Rohingya history, Islamic Studies, mother-tongue instruction, practical science and digital literacy. A standardised assessment and certification mechanism should also be introduced to improve educational accountability and facilitate future academic progression.

Community-run madrasas constitute another important pillar of education within the camps. Although comprehensive and independently verified information about their number and enrolment remains limited, their contribution to educational access and religious and cultural preservation is substantial. However, many predominantly follow traditional Deobandi curricula, with insufficient emphasis on contemporary subjects such as science, mathematics, information technology and critical thinking. Urdu remains a principal medium of instruction in many institutions, although its practical relevance to future reintegration into Myanmar is limited. A more appropriate approach would integrate religious education with the Myanmar Curriculum, Burmese and English language instruction, and digital literacy.

Perhaps the most critical structural gap concerns secondary, tertiary and higher education. Rohingya students completing available educational programmes have extremely limited opportunities to pursue accredited university education or higher learning. The absence of structured pathways through scholarships, vocational institutions, distance learning and accredited online degree programmes leaves many academically capable young people without meaningful opportunities to develop their potential. This represents not only an individual educational disadvantage but also a considerable loss of human capital that could contribute to Myanmar's future reconstruction.

The emerging risk of a lost generation

The Rohingya education crisis extends beyond limited access to classrooms. The deprioritisation of education within the humanitarian response, declining funding and the absence of credible assessment and certification mechanisms threaten to undermine learners' motivation and accelerate educational disengagement.

For adolescents and young people, the problem is particularly acute. They face severely restricted opportunities for higher education, recognised qualifications, skills development and meaningful employment. When education offers no credible progression pathway, students and their families may increasingly question the value of continued participation. This creates the conditions for a potential lost generation: young people who have neither acquired sufficient education and skills nor obtained recognised qualifications to demonstrate their achievements.

An equally serious concern relates to identity, culture and collective knowledge. Educational exclusion is not simply the denial of access to classrooms; it may also involve the gradual erosion of opportunities to preserve and transmit a community's history, language, cultural heritage and collective memory. For a displaced and stateless community such as the Rohingya, prolonged separation from their homeland, combined with insufficient institutional space for preserving indigenous knowledge, may weaken intergenerational connections with their historical roots.

This paper therefore introduces the concept of epistemicide to understand this deeper dimension of educational deprivation. Here, epistemicide refers to the gradual erosion of a community's capacity to preserve, reproduce and transmit its own knowledge, history, identity and collective memory across generations. It may emerge through the cumulative effects of displacement, cultural marginalisation, educational exclusion and the absence of sustainable intellectual and social development opportunities.

Without urgent intervention, an entire generation risks becoming trapped between a fading connection to its past and an uncertain future. Preventing this outcome requires an educational strategy that recognises both the instrumental value of education for future reintegration and its intrinsic importance in preserving the Rohingya people's collective identity.
Rohingya students interact with the Duchess of Edinburgh during her visit to Cox’s Bazar. The encounter highlights the importance of sustained international support for quality education, higher learning opportunities and skills development to prevent a lost generation of Rohingya youth. Photo: Prabir Das

RRRC's strategic initiatives to strengthen preparedness for sustainable repatriation

Recognising the challenges of prolonged displacement, the RRRC has undertaken several initiatives aimed at preserving Rohingya identity, strengthening community resilience and sustaining the aspiration for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable repatriation.

Preserving cultural identity and collective memory

The RRRC has encouraged humanitarian partners to incorporate Rohingya history, identity and cultural heritage into educational and community activities. Various extracurricular programmes, including Hamd and Na'at competitions, Qur'an recitation, Adhan competitions, cultural performances, drawing competitions, essay writing and art exhibitions, have been organised around themes such as Dreaming of Justice, What I Miss Most, My Right to Return, Rohingya Festivals and Traditions, Rebuilding My Homeland and Our Livelihood in Myanmar.

A desk calendar featuring artwork by competition winners has been produced, while photographs documenting significant events and activities have been compiled into a commemorative photobook. Beyond their artistic value, these initiatives contribute to preserving collective memories, strengthening cultural consciousness and maintaining emotional connections with the homeland.

Sports, youth engagement and community solidarity

The RRRC has also promoted sports and youth engagement as instruments of social development, psychosocial well-being and community solidarity. Large-scale football and Cylloyne tournaments organised across the camps have attracted considerable participation.

Importantly, participating teams have been named after Rohingya-dominated localities in their homeland, including Rathedaung, Buthidaung and Maungdaw. This approach reinforces younger generations' connections with their places of origin and sustains awareness of their historical and geographical roots. Such activities provide constructive recreational opportunities while encouraging youth leadership, hope and a shared vision of returning to their homeland.

Establishing institutional platforms for historical preservation

The RRRC has facilitated several initiatives dedicated to preserving Rohingya history, heritage and collective knowledge.

The Rohingya Center, established in Balukhali Camp 10, provides a platform for documenting the community's history, culture, heritage, political representation and prolonged persecution. Similarly, the Rohang Heritage Center in Camp 6 seeks to preserve the cultural heritage, political legacy and historical identity of the Rohingya people.

In addition, the RRRC, in collaboration with the Centre for Peace and Justice (CPJ), BRAC University, has facilitated the establishment of the Rohingya History and Knowledge Centre (RHKC) in Camp 17. These institutional platforms provide opportunities for children, adolescents and young people to engage with their history, cultural heritage and collective memory through educational, artistic and community activities.

Together, these initiatives seek to ensure that displacement does not result in the disappearance of a people's historical consciousness and that future generations remain connected to their identity and aspirations for returning to Arakan (Rakhine State) with dignity and justice.
Rohingya children participate in learning activities at a centre in Kutupalong camp, Cox’s Bazar. Expanding access to quality education, recognised qualifications and skills development is essential to preparing young refugees for eventual repatriation and the reconstruction of their homeland. Photo: UNHCR/Vincent Tremeau

Facilitating strategic educational partnerships and innovation

Beyond its own initiatives, the RRRC has played an important facilitating role in expanding educational opportunities through partnerships with national, international and community-led institutions.

The RRRC has facilitated educational initiatives involving the Asian University for Women (AUW) and UNICEF-supported teacher development programmes. It allocated a Multipurpose Centre in Camp 4 Extension for a dedicated teacher training centre, providing administrative and logistical support to strengthen teachers' pedagogical capacities.

The RRRC maintains the position that Bangla should not be introduced as the medium of instruction in the Rohingya camps. Instead, educational arrangements should remain oriented towards future reintegration into Myanmar, with Burmese and English serving as the principal languages of instruction in learning centres.

Recognising the limited Burmese-language proficiency of many Rohingya teachers, the RRRC encouraged UNESCO to strengthen its engagement in teacher capacity development. UNESCO subsequently prioritised available resources for Burmese language training for teachers, support for volunteer teacher stipends and essential educational operations.

The RRRC has also supported the UNHCR–Bard College Programme and emerging digital education initiatives implemented by American Muslim organisations, thereby broadening opportunities for higher learning, digital literacy, leadership development and career-oriented skills.

Supporting community-led education

One notable example of community-led educational development is the Rohingya National Education Board (RNEB), a non-profit educational body established in 2017 to preserve and promote the Rohingya language through the Hanifi script, culture and identity. Its activities include language education, curriculum development, teacher training, examinations and certification. With the facilitation and enabling environment provided by the RRRC, RNEB has expanded to more than 33,000 students across 325 learning centres and community schools in 2026.

Another important development is the establishment of the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees (EBRR) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The initiative addresses a longstanding gap in assessment and certification among community-led schools. Beginning with 75 participating schools, the network expanded to 116 institutions during the 2026–2027 academic year. Through standardised midterm and final examinations, transparent publication of results and recognition of academic achievement, EBRR is contributing to improved educational accountability and learner motivation.

The RRRC has also facilitated the continuation of the Myanmar National Curriculum through community-led schools operated by Rohingya volunteer educators and community leaders. By 2026, the initiative encompassed 219 schools, approximately 54,750 students and 2,190 volunteer teachers. Technical volunteers, zonal supervisors, advisory committees and camp education committees have further strengthened educational coordination and community participation.

Collectively, these partnerships demonstrate that the RRRC's contribution extends beyond conventional administrative oversight. By bringing together international organisations, academic institutions, donors and community-led educational bodies, it has helped develop a diversified educational ecosystem encompassing formal, non-formal, digital, tertiary, linguistic and cultural learning opportunities.
Ek Khaale: Once Upon a Time, an exhibition curated by Greg Constantine and organised by BRAC University’s Centre for Peace and Justice in August 2025, explored Rohingya history, identity and collective memory through archival materials, photographs and historical dialogues, highlighting the importance of cultural preservation amid prolonged displacement. Photo courtesy: Greg Constantine

Policy recommendations for the Government of Bangladesh

Drawing upon the experiences of the past decade, Bangladesh should consider complementing its diplomatic efforts with a comprehensive educational and human capital development strategy. Bilateral agreements alone cannot guarantee successful repatriation. Sustainable return ultimately depends on political conditions in Myanmar, security, citizenship, justice, rights and the confidence, preparedness and collective agency of the Rohingya people.

The following strategic priorities merit consideration:

First, institutionalise a comprehensive education framework. The government should strengthen existing RRRC-facilitated initiatives and promote consistent implementation of the Myanmar Curriculum, supplemented by Rohingya history, language, Islamic Studies, practical science and digital literacy. A credible assessment and certification framework should be developed across learning centres and community-led schools to ensure that educational achievements can be demonstrated and recognised.

Second, expand secondary, tertiary and vocational opportunities. Accredited online degree programmes, distance learning, international scholarships, vocational institutions and partnerships with national and international universities should be promoted. These opportunities would help develop future professionals, educators, researchers and community leaders capable of contributing to Myanmar's reconstruction.

Third, pursue educational and cultural diplomacy. Bangladesh could explore scholarship opportunities for outstanding Rohingya students and, where appropriate, students from other ethnic communities in Rakhine State. Academic exchanges, joint research, cultural programmes and institutional partnerships could gradually establish educational and professional linkages between Bangladesh and Rakhine State. Engagement involving writers, artists, academics, researchers, religious scholars and civil society representatives could also contribute to mutual understanding and peaceful coexistence.

Fourth, strengthen international engagement on justice and accountability. The forthcoming ICJ judgment on 19 November 2026 provides an important opportunity to renew international attention to the Rohingya crisis. Bangladesh should continue to advocate for accountability, recognition of Rohingya rights and effective implementation of relevant international legal obligations. The judgment should be considered within a broader diplomatic strategy that connects justice and accountability with the creation of conditions necessary for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable repatriation. International legal developments must also be accompanied by practical diplomatic engagement with relevant stakeholders in Myanmar and the wider international community.

Fifth, promote human capital development as part of future reconstruction. Bangladesh could share its expertise in agriculture, fisheries, livestock, public health, engineering, housing, disaster risk reduction and rural development to support the socioeconomic recovery of a peaceful Rakhine State. The knowledge and skills developed among Rohingya youth in Bangladesh should be recognised as a potential resource for the future reconstruction of their homeland.

Finally, strengthen international responsibility-sharing. The declining availability of humanitarian resources should not undermine the educational prospects of an entire generation. The international community must sustain investment in education, infrastructure, livelihoods, healthcare and institutional capacity, both within the refugee response and in areas of potential return. Ensuring that returnees have access to education, security, citizenship, equal rights and sustainable livelihood opportunities will be essential to preventing renewed displacement.

Through these interconnected measures, Bangladesh could contribute more proactively to shaping the conditions for peaceful reintegration and long-term stability in Rakhine State, without compromising its consistent position against permanent local integration of the displaced population.
Limited access to education, recognised qualifications and employment opportunities leaves many Rohingya adolescents facing an uncertain future. Prolonged educational exclusion risks increasing their vulnerability to exploitation, criminal recruitment and other harmful activities, underscoring the urgency of investing in meaningful learning and skills development. Photo: Aeer Shaad

Conclusion

After nearly a decade of displacement, the Rohingya crisis can no longer be addressed solely through humanitarian assistance. The sustainability of any future repatriation process will depend not only on political agreements and security guarantees but also on the preparedness, knowledge, identity, resilience and aspirations of the Rohingya people.

The forthcoming judgment of the International Court of Justice in The Gambia v. Myanmar on 19 November 2026 may mark an important milestone in the pursuit of justice and accountability. However, justice must ultimately be accompanied by practical conditions that enable the Rohingya to return voluntarily and rebuild their lives with dignity, security and recognised rights.

The experiences documented in this paper demonstrate that Bangladesh, through the facilitative leadership of the RRRC, has moved beyond conventional emergency education by supporting innovative partnerships, community-led educational institutions, cultural preservation, language development and emerging opportunities for higher and digital education. These initiatives provide an important foundation for preventing a lost generation and nurturing educated, skilled and responsible Rohingya youth capable of contributing to the future reconstruction of Myanmar.

Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, particularly declining humanitarian funding, limited higher education opportunities, curricular gaps, inadequate certification mechanisms and prolonged uncertainty. Addressing these challenges requires sustained international responsibility-sharing, stronger institutional coordination and greater investment in quality education and human capital development.

Ultimately, sustainable repatriation will require more than the restoration of the legal right to return. It will require a generation equipped with the education, skills, confidence, cultural identity and leadership necessary to rebuild its homeland. Investing in Rohingya education today is therefore not merely an investment in refugee welfare; it is an investment in justice, sustainable repatriation, the future reconstruction of Myanmar and lasting regional stability.

Mohammed Mizanur Rahman is an additional secretary to the Government of Bangladesh, currently serving as the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner (RRRC) in Cox’s Bazar.

Md Aftabuzzaman Al Imran holds an MA in Development Studies from the Institute of Development Studies (IDS) at the University of Sussex.

Its activities include language education, curriculum development, teacher training, examinations and certification. With the facilitation and enabling environment provided by the RRRC, RNEB has expanded to more than 33,000 students across 325 learning centres and community schools in 2026.

Another important development is the establishment of the Examination Board of Rohingya Refugees (EBRR) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The initiative addresses a longstanding gap in assessment and certification among community-led schools. Beginning with 75 participating schools, the network expanded to 116 institutions during the 2026–2027 academic year. Through standardised midterm and final examinations, transparent publication of results and recognition of academic achievement, EBRR is contributing to improved educational accountability and learner motivation.

The RRRC has also facilitated the continuation of the Myanmar National Curriculum through community-led schools operated by Rohingya volunteer educators and community leaders. By 2026, the initiative encompassed 219 schools, approximately 54,750 students and 2,190 volunteer teachers. Technical volunteers, zonal supervisors, advisory committees and camp education committees have further strengthened educational coordination and community participation.

Collectively, these partnerships demonstrate that the RRRC's contribution extends beyond conventional administrative oversight. By bringing together international organisations, academic institutions, donors and community-led educational bodies, it has helped develop a diversified educational ecosystem encompassing formal, non-formal, digital, tertiary, linguistic and cultural learning opportunities.
Ek Khaale: Once Upon a Time, an exhibition curated by Greg Constantine and organised by BRAC University’s Centre for Peace and Justice in August 2025, explored Rohingya history, identity and collective memory through archival materials, photographs and historical dialogues, highlighting the importance of cultural preservation amid prolonged displacement. Photo courtesy: Greg Constantine

Policy recommendations for the Government of Bangladesh

Drawing upon the experiences of the past decade, Bangladesh should consider complementing its diplomatic efforts with a comprehensive educational and human capital development strategy. Bilateral agreements alone cannot guarantee successful repatriation. Sustainable return ultimately depends on political conditions in Myanmar, security, citizenship, justice, rights and the confidence, preparedness and collective agency of the Rohingya people.

The following strategic priorities merit consideration:

First, institutionalise a comprehensive education framework. The government should strengthen existing RRRC-facilitated initiatives and promote consistent implementation of the Myanmar Curriculum, supplemented by Rohingya history, language, Islamic Studies, practical science and digital literacy. A credible assessment and certification framework should be developed across learning centres and community-led schools to ensure that educational achievements can be demonstrated and recognised.

Second, expand secondary, tertiary and vocational opportunities. Accredited online degree programmes, distance learning, international scholarships, vocational institutions and partnerships with national and international universities should be promoted. These opportunities would help develop future professionals, educators, researchers and community leaders capable of contributing to Myanmar's reconstruction.

Third, pursue educational and cultural diplomacy. Bangladesh could explore scholarship opportunities for outstanding Rohingya students and, where appropriate, students from other ethnic communities in Rakhine State. Academic exchanges, joint research, cultural programmes and institutional partnerships could gradually establish educational and professional linkages between Bangladesh and Rakhine State. Engagement involving writers, artists, academics, researchers, religious scholars and civil society representatives could also contribute to mutual understanding and peaceful coexistence.

Fourth, strengthen international engagement on justice and accountability. The forthcoming ICJ judgment on 19 November 2026 provides an important opportunity to renew international attention to the Rohingya crisis. Bangladesh should continue to advocate for accountability, recognition of Rohingya rights and effective implementation of relevant international legal obligations. The judgment should be considered within a broader diplomatic strategy that connects justice and accountability with the creation of conditions necessary for voluntary, safe, dignified and sustainable repatriation. International legal developments must also be accompanied by practical diplomatic engagement with relevant stakeholders in Myanmar and the wider international community.

Fifth, promote human capital development as part of future reconstruction. Bangladesh could share its expertise in agriculture, fisheries, livestock, public health, engineering, housing, disaster risk reduction and rural development to support the socioeconomic recovery of a peaceful Rakhine State. The knowledge and skills developed among Rohingya youth in Bangladesh should be recognised as a potential resource for the future reconstruction of their homeland.

Finally, strengthen international responsibility-sharing. The declining availability of humanitarian resources should not undermine the educational prospects of an entire generation. The international community must sustain investment in education, infrastructure, livelihoods, healthcare and institutional capacity, both within the refugee response and in areas of potential return. Ensuring that returnees have access to education, security, citizenship, equal rights and sustainable livelihood opportunities will be essential to preventing renewed displacement.

Through these interconnected measures, Bangladesh could contribute more proactively to shaping the conditions for peaceful reintegration and long-term stability in Rakhine State, without compromising its consistent position against permanent local integration of the displaced population.
Limited access to education, recognised qualifications and employment opportunities leaves many Rohingya adolescents facing an uncertain future. Prolonged educational exclusion risks increasing their vulnerability to exploitation, criminal recruitment and other harmful activities, underscoring the urgency of investing in meaningful learning and skills development. Photo: Aeer Shaad

Conclusion

After nearly a decade of displacement, the Rohingya crisis can no longer be addressed solely through humanitarian assistance. The sustainability of any future repatriation process will depend not only on political agreements and security guarantees but also on the preparedness, knowledge, identity, resilience and aspirations of the Rohingya people.

The forthcoming judgment of the International Court of Justice in The Gambia v. Myanmar on 19 November 2026 may mark an important milestone in the pursuit of justice and accountability. However, justice must ultimately be accompanied by practical conditions that enable the Rohingya to return voluntarily and rebuild their lives with dignity, security and recognised rights.

The experiences documented in this paper demonstrate that Bangladesh, through the facilitative leadership of the RRRC, has moved beyond conventional emergency education by supporting innovative partnerships, community-led educational institutions, cultural preservation, language development and emerging opportunities for higher and digital education. These initiatives provide an important foundation for preventing a lost generation and nurturing educated, skilled and responsible Rohingya youth capable of contributing to the future reconstruction of Myanmar.

Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, particularly declining humanitarian funding, limited higher education opportunities, curricular gaps, inadequate certification mechanisms and prolonged uncertainty. Addressing these challenges requires sustained international responsibility-sharing, stronger institutional coordination and greater investment in quality education and human capital development.

Ultimately, sustainable repatriation will require more than the restoration of the legal right to return. It will require a generation equipped with the education, skills, confidence, cultural identity and leadership necessary to rebuild its homeland. Investing in Rohingya education today is therefore not merely an investment in refugee welfare; it is an investment in justice, sustainable repatriation, the future reconstruction of Myanmar and lasting regional stability.
